text: Before Zerobus, ingesting high-volume event data meant the producing application wrote to a message bus like Kafka, and a separate Spark Structured Streaming job read from that bus into Delta. Zerobus Ingest is a set of APIs that let a producing application push event data directly into a Delta table instead.

That's the whole architectural shift: producer to message bus to Spark Streaming to Delta, versus producer straight to the Zerobus API to Delta. When the lakehouse is the only destination for this data, that middle hop was pure overhead — extra infrastructure to run, monitor, and pay for.

These are Databricks' own published specs, not estimates. Ingestion latency is near real-time, under five seconds. A single client can push up to 100 megabytes per second, with thousands of concurrent clients writing to the same table. And once data lands in Delta, the real-time ForeachWriter pattern can sync it to Lakebase in 200 to 300 milliseconds.

The entire client-side surface is two steps: authenticate with OAuth and open a stream, then ingest records on that open stream. No topic configuration, no partition count to choose, no consumer group to manage — and it still writes through Unity Catalog governance, using the exact same GRANT pattern from Chapter 1.

As of this writing, Zerobus Ingest does not support Change Data Feed on the table it writes to directly. If your downstream use case needs CDF — syncing to Lakebase, for example — the documented workaround is to stream the Zerobus target table into a second Delta table with CDF enabled. This is a real, current product gap, worth naming explicitly.
Next lesson: Lakebase — how that Delta data gets served back out to a real-time operational application, without a hand-built reverse-ETL pipeline.
